CHEM CHEM Hybrid Deep Eutectic Solvents with Flexible Hydrogen-Bonded Supramolecular Networks for Highly Efficient Uptake of NH3 Yuhui Li, Mohammad Chand Ali, Qiwei Yang,* Zhiguo Zhang, Zongbi Bao, Baogen Su, Huabin Xing, and Qilong Ren[a]

Serious environmental concerns have led to a great demand for efficient uptake of NH3 by solvents. However, traditional aqueous absorbents have many shortcomings and efforts to use ionic liquids have met with limited success. A hybrid deep eutectic solvents (DESs) designed with a flexible hydrogen-bonded supramolecular network exhibits both exceptional NH3 uptake capacity and superior desorption-regeneration performance, along with superb NH3/CO2 selectivity and environmental merit. Elucidated by molecular dynamic simulations and spectroscopic analysis, the abundant hydrogen-bonding sites in the hybrid DESs bind every atom of the NH3 molecule

and enable strong physical reversible solvation, whereas the multiple interactions among the hybrid components create a flexible hydrogen-bonded supramolecular network and allow for solvent-unbreaking absorption to ensure the full participa- tion of the solvent and process stability. A mass solubility of NH3 up to 0.13 gg⁻¹ was achieved at 313 K and 101 kPa by the hybrid DES choline chloride/resorcinol/glycerol (1:3:5), which is higher than all reported ionic liquids and ordinary DESs. More- over, the performance remained the same after ten absorp- tion-desorption cycles and the DESs could be easily regenerat- ed.

# Introduction Global challenges in environmental and sustainable chemistry have created a great demand for efficient uptake of NH3 from the gas phase, because NH3 is not only a major alkaline gaseous atmospheric pollutant and an important precursor of PM2.5 (particulate matter ≤2.5 µm), but also the dominant working medium in low-hazard Freon-free absorption refrigerators.[1] The omnipresent absorbents in current NH3 capture plants and refrigerators are water and aqueous inorganic or carboxylic acids, which have suffered from lots of longstanding problems.[2] First, the high volatility of water and many acids and the strong reactivity of NH3 with those solvents incurs significant difficulties to the desorption of NH3 and recycle of absorbents, making the energy-intensive distillation and a complex process usually indispensable in the plants and refrigerators.[3] Moreover, strong corrosion of equipment by the absorbents often occurs, and the wastewater discharge is hard to avoid. A lot of efforts have been exerted to address these problems, especially the utilization of ionic liquids as low-volatile solvents in absorption.[4] However, limited success has been achieved owing to the unsatisfactory mass solubility of NH3

In recent years, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been put forward as a new class of solvents[6] that share the advantages of ultralow volatility and designability of ionic liquids and are superior in price, synthesis, and biodegradability.[6e] However, one chemical characteristic of DESs that is distinct from common solvents and ionic liquids is that they are supramolecular complexes of different individual components rather than a "pure" substance.[7] Therefore, DESs are more "fragile" liquids and their structure may decompose into individual components if there is a strong interaction with other solvents or solutes. Unfortunately, this fragile nature of DESs has not been paid enough attention up to now, although it is essential for their practical performance. An attempt to increase the efficiency of a DES for dissolving a solute by enhancing the DES-solute interactions, which is the common-sense strategy for ordinary solvents and ionic liquids, will probably fail because the enhanced DES-solute interactions may also break up the supramolecular structure of the DES and generate nonfunctional solids. This trade-off between the DES-solute interactions and the DES stability is particularly significant if the solute molecules are very active, as is the case for NH3 (Figure 1).

## Results and Discussion ### NH3 absorption Several widely used ordinary DESs, which were binary mixtures of choline chloride (ChCl) and different hydrogen bond donors (HBDs), were first tested for the absorption of NH3 at 313 K and 101 kPa (Figure 1). White solids quickly appeared during the absorption by DESs with acidic HBDs (phenols and carboxylic acids), which severely inhibited the contact of NH3 with the remaining absorbent and prevented the continuation of the absorption process. FTIR measurement of these solids revealed that they were almost pure phenols (Figure 1 d, exemplified by the absorption of 1:3 ChCl/resorcinol), indicating that the solid formation is caused by the breaking up of the supramolecular structure in the DES. The adverse effect of this phenomenon is well demonstrated by the abnormal acidity-capacity relationship in the absorption by those solvents. Given that phenols and carboxylic acids are much more acidic than alcohols and urea, the NH3 uptake capacities of DESs containing phenols and carboxylic acids were expected to be higher than those of ChCl/Gly, ChCl/EG, and ChCl/Ur. However, these expected results were not observed. The NH3 uptake capacity of ChCl/PhA was lower than that of ChCl/Gly. Moreover, although resorcinol contains more hydroxy groups than phenol and is also more acidic (the respective pKa values of resorcinol and phenol are 9.44 and 9.94), the NH3 uptake capacity of ChCl/Res (0.053 g g¯¹) was unexpectedly much lower than that of ChCl/Phe (0.081 g g¯¹) owing to the more extensive formation of solids. This abnormal acidity-capacity relationship indicated that, because of the fragile supramolecular structure of DESs, the well-acknowledged strategy to enhance the solubility of basic solutes by increasing the acidity or the number of acidic groups of the solvents is not necessarily valid in the case of DESs. The use of neutral HBDs instead of phenols and carboxylic acids can prevent this structural breakage to ensure a “complete” absorption, but the reduced solute-solvent interactions also reduces the NH3 uptake capacity.

To address the trade-off between the NH3-DES interaction and the supramolecular stability, we prepared a novel class of hybrid DESs, which was formed from a ternary mixture of chol- ine chloride, phenolic compounds, and polyalcohol and can be deemed as a hybrid of two binary DESs (choline chloride + phenolic compound and choline chloride + polyalcohol). Com- pared with ordinary DESs, the hybrid DESs reached a high level of NH3 solubility without the precipitation of solids. The uptake capacities of NH3 in choline chloride/phenol/ethylene glycol (1:3:5, molar ratio, ChCl/Phe/EG) and choline chloride/ phenol/glycerol (1:3:5, molar ratio, ChCl/Phe/Gly) at 313 K and 101 kPa were 0.091 gg⁻¹ and 0.095 gg⁻¹, respectively, which were superior to the related binary analogues, ChCl/Phe (0.082 gg⁻¹) and ChCl/Gly (0.053 gg⁻¹). More notably, when phenol in ChCl/Phe/Gly was replaced by resorcinol, the NH3 solubility in ChCl/Res/Gly (1:3:5 molar ratio) improved further

Among the various investigated ionic liquids in earlier reports of NH₃ absorption, [4b,g] 1-hydroxyethyli-midazolium tetrafluoroborate ([EtOHmim][BF₄]) showed the highest NH₃ mass solubility. However, the value at 313 K and 101 kPa was 0.051 g g⁻¹ (Figure 1a), which was only 39% of that in ChCl/Res/Gly. The other top-performing ionic liquids had even lower mass solubilities, 0.036 g g⁻¹ for 1-hydroxye-thylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethane)sulfonimide ([EtOHmim][NTf₂]) and 0.042 g g⁻¹ for 1-hydroxyethylimidazolium hexa-fluorophosphate ([EtOHmim][PF₆]).

Table 1 lists all of the ionic liquids that have been reported for NH3 absorption and the units of the solubilities were unified in g(NH3)g(solvent)⁻¹. The NH3 solubilities in all those ionic liquids were lower than that in ChCl/Res/Gly under the same conditions. By comparing the NH3 solubilities among different ionic liquids, the incorporation of hydroxy or an acidic Nδ⁺–H group in ionic liquids was found to be essential for higher solubilities, which is also the reason for the high NH3 capacity of DES. The number density of hydroxy groups in ChCl/Res/Gly (0.024 molg⁻¹) was much higher than that in hydroxy-containing ionic liquids (e.g, 0.0047 molg⁻¹ in [EtOHmim][BF4], 0.0025 molg⁻¹ in [EtOHmim][NTf2], 0.0037 molg⁻¹ in [EtOHmim][PF6]). We also measured the hydrogen-bond acidity (α) of ChCl/Res/Gly using Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic method, and obtained a value of 2.87. This signifies the stronger hydrogen-bond acidity of ChCl/Res/Gly than ionic liquids (e.g., the α of [EtOHmim][NTf2] is 1.14).[9] Thus, the stronger ability of ChCl/Res/Gly than ionic liquids to dissolve NH3 can be ascribed to the higher abundance of hydroxy groups and higher hydro-

gen-bond acidity. In a very recent report, 1-butylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide ([Bim][NTf2]) was reported to show NH3 mass solubility close to ChCl/Res/Gly, which resulted from the presence of acidic Nδ+-H groups. [4a] Nevertheless, the [NTf2]--based ionic liquids are generally expensive for practical applications.

Promising results were obtained even when compared with the absorption of NH3 by water, which has an NH3 solubility of 0.30 gg⁻¹ at 313 K 101 kPa. [10] Although this value is somewhat higher than the NH3 capacity of DESs, the use of water or aqueous solutions as solvents has serious shortcomings, espe- cially for the desorption of NH3 and regeneration of solvents that are crucial in industrial applications. [2, 3b,c, 11] If hybrid DESs are employed as solvents, an NH3 solubility comparable to that of a water system could be achieved, and the absorbent could be easily regenerated by a simple evaporation at moderate temperature while the desorbed NH3 is obtained without con- tamination of the absorbent. Typically, the desorption and re- generation of DES were investigated for ChCI/Res/Gly. NH3 was adsorbed until saturation at 313 K and 101 kPa, and then was descrbed with a vacuum pump for 5 h at 323 K. Ten absorp- tion–desorption cycles were performed without the loss of uptake capacity (Figure 2), which suggested a recyclability very superior to aqueous solvents. Consequently, the results dem- onstrated that the proposed hybrid DESs not only have an ad- vantage over conventional ionic liquids, but are also very promising even compared with aqueous absorption.

Moreover, when the molar ratio further changed to 1:10:5, there was no DES generated after mixing of the three components. These results indicate the phenols played an important role in capturing NH3 molecule, but excessive phenols would reduce the supramolecular stability of DESs during absorption and even inhibit the formation of a DES.

If polyalcohols were absent from the DES, the resultant ChCl/Phe was also poor at adsorbing NH3, as described previ- ously. To further investigate the effect of the polyalcohol con- tent, ChCl/Phe/Gly with molar ratios of 1:3:1, 1:3:3, and 1:3:5 were applied to NH3 absorption at 313 K and 101 kPa. The ex- periments showed that the NH3 absorption capacity of the DES with ChCl/Phe/Gly molar ratios of 1:3:3 and 1:3:5 were 0.096 gg⁻¹ and 0.095 gg⁻¹, respectively, whereas many white

solids were generated and the capacity was 0.071 gg⁻¹ if the molar ratio was 1:3:1. If DESs with ChCl/Res/Gly molar ratios of 1:3:1 and 1:3:3 were employed for NH₃ absorption at 313 K and 101 kPa, there was a tremendous amount of white solids formed and the mixture could not be stirred. If the molar ratio of ChCl/Res/Gly was 1:3:5, the solvent remained clear and transparent after NH₃ saturation. These results indicated that glycerol was necessary to prevent the breakdown of the supra-molecular structure of the DESs to ensure the maximum ab-sorption, but excess glycerol also decreased the NH₃ capacity. The minimum amount of glycerol required to prevent the for-mation of solid was different between phenol and resorcinol. To shed light on this phenomenon, other analogous phenols including catechol and phloroglucinol were used to prepare DESs to further investigate the NH₃ absorption. For catechol, which is an isomer of resorcinol, if a choline chloride/catechol/glycerol molar ratio of 1:3:5 was used the NH₃ uptake capacity was 0.12 gg⁻¹ capacity and a clear solution was obtained. If the molar ratio of choline chloride/catechol/glycerol was 1:3:3, solids formed and the solution was murky. These results were very similar to those observed for resorcinol with the same molar ratio. Thus, with the increase of the amount of hydroxy groups, the choline chloride/phenols/glycerol system formed more solids when NH₃ was dissolved, and the minimum amount of glycerol required to prevent the formation of solids was higher. As expected, although choline chloride/phloroglu-cinol/glycerol in a molar ratio 1:3:5 was liquid, there was a large amount of white solid formed as soon as NH₃ was bub-bled into the solution. The absorption process subsequently stopped and a low NH₃ solubility was obtained. However, the DES with a choline chloride/hydroquinone/glycerol molar ratio of 1:3:5 and 1:3:9 was solid under ambient conditions. This un-expected result suggested the significance of the location of the hydroxy group in the phenols in the formation of a DES. Hydroquinone had the highest melting point among the three isomers (resorcinol (Tₘ=384 K), catechol (Tₘ=378 K) and hy-droquinone (Tₘ=445 K), which may account for the failed syn-thesis of the choline chloride/hydroquinone/glycerol DES.

Choline chloride was also essential. When choline chloride was absent, the resultant solvent was volatile, showing a re- markable loss of weight during desorption, whereas the weight change of the ChCl/Phe/Gly and ChCl/Res/Gly DESs were negligible under the same conditions even after ten ab- sorption–desorption cycles.

NMR spectroscopy ¹H NMR spectroscopy was performed for fresh ChCl/Res/Gly, NH₃-dissolved ChCl/Res/Gly, and the regenerated ChCl/Res/Gly after ten absorption–desorption cycles (Figure 7, Figures S2–S4 in the Supporting Information). After dissolving NH₃, the peaks at δ = 9.17, 5.36, 4.42, and 4.50 ppm in the fresh ChCl/Res/Gly disappeared, whereas a very broad flat peak appeared in the range of δ = 5.49–3.77 ppm. Then, when the dissolved NH₃ was removed, even after ten absorption–desorption cycles, the spectrum of the regenerated ChCl/Res/Gly returned to be almost the same as that of fresh ChCl/Res/Gly, except that the peaks at δ = 9.17, 5.36, 4.42, and 4.50 ppm were much wider than in the fresh one; the integrals of these peaks did not change. The peak at δ = 9.17 ppm was assigned to the hydroxy H in resorcinol, and the peaks at δ = 5.36, 4.42, and 4.50 ppm were assigned to the hydroxy H in choline chloride and glycerol. Thus, these results confirm two points. First, the absorption of NH₃ did not decompose the ChCl/Res/Gly, and the dissolved NH₃ had strong hydrogen-bond interactions with the hydroxy H atoms in ChCl/Res/Gly. Second, consistent with the regeneration experiments, the absorption of NH₃ in ChCl/Res/Gly was readily reversible and recyclable by simple evaporation. The broader hydroxy H peaks after desorption probably arise from a reconstruction of the local microstructure in the solvent.

## Conclusions In this work, a new method to capture NH3 from gas phase with high efficiency has been proposed by using hybrid DESs as absorbents. The essence of this method is the construction of hybrid DESs with a flexible hydrogen-bonded supramolecular network, which enables the strong physical reversible solvation of NH3 and removes the need for a trade-off between the strength of the NH3–DES interactions and the stability of the supramolecular structure. Consequently, both exceptional NH3 mass capacity and excellent desorption–regeneration performance were achieved by this method, along with superb NH3/CO2 selectivity and environmental merit. Furthermore, taking into account their easy synthesis, relativity low cost, and good biocompatibility, the hybrid DESs have great potential as efficient and green alternatives to aqueous solvents and ionic liquids in practical NH3 capture and separation processes. Additionally, considering that the fragility of the supramolecular structure is an intrinsic character of ordinary DESs, this work is also important for the application of DESs in more processes.

## Computational method MD simulations were run with the GROMACS 4.5.4,[14] software package. Partial atomic charges were derived from the optimized geometry using the restrained electrostatic potential (RESP) method with the R.E.D.-III.4 package.[15] To control the pressure and temperature in the NPT ensemble, a name for the isothermal–iso- baric ensemble where the number of particles (N), pressure (P), and temperature (T) of the system are specified, the Berendsen barostat method with a relaxation time of 0.5 ps and the V-rescale thermostat method (313 K for all simulations) with a relaxation time of 0.1 ps were applied. The ChCl/Res/Gly simulation system was composed of 100 pairs of ChCl/Res/Gly (1:3:5 molar ratio). The ChCl/Res/Gly–NH3 simulation system was composed of 100 pairs of ChCl/Res/Gly–NH3 (1:3:5:7 molar ratio). An AMBER force field was adopted in this paper. The system was equilibrated for 2 ns in the NPT ensemble, and the last 1 ns was used to collect data for the radial distribution function and energy analysis. The forcefield pa- rameterization used in this work was validated through the com- parison of the predicted physical property, density, with the experi- mental value. The density of ChCl/Res/Gly obtained experimentally was approximately 1.21 gcm⁻³ at 313 K 101 kPa, whereas the den- sity obtained from MD was 1.24 g cm⁻³. Likewise, the experimental density of ChCl/Res/Gly–NH3 was approximately 1.14 g cm⁻³ at 313 K 101 kPa, whereas the density obtained from MD was 1.20 g cm⁻³. The deviation between the data was less than 7%, which is acceptable and shows the suitable performance of the used parameterization for describing the microscopic information. A complete listing of all the relevant force field parameters and partial charges is provided in Table S1.

Check for updates <::logo: ChemPubSoc Europe ChemPubSoc Europe Stylized checkmark inside a circle surrounded by stars, resembling a European Union flag motif.::> DOI: 10.1002/cssc.201701135 <::logo: ChemSusChem CHEMSUSTCHEM Full Papers The logo features the word "CHEMSUSTCHEM" in a dark grey serif font, with "SUS" highlighted in a teal color, and "Full Papers" in a lighter grey sans-serif font below.::> CHEM CHEM Hybrid Deep Eutectic Solvents with Flexible Hydrogen-Bonded Supramolecular Networks for Highly Efficient Uptake of NH3 Yuhui Li, Mohammad Chand Ali, Qiwei Yang,* Zhiguo Zhang, Zongbi Bao, Baogen Su, Huabin Xing, and Qilong Ren[a] Serious environmental concerns have led to a great demand for efficient uptake of NH3 by solvents. However, traditional aqueous absorbents have many shortcomings and efforts to use ionic liquids have met with limited success. A hybrid deep eutectic solvents (DESs) designed with a flexible hydrogen-bonded supramolecular network exhibits both exceptional NH3 uptake capacity and superior desorption-regeneration performance, along with superb NH3/CO2 selectivity and environmental merit. Elucidated by molecular dynamic simulations and spectroscopic analysis, the abundant hydrogen-bonding sites in the hybrid DESs bind every atom of the NH3 molecule and enable strong physical reversible solvation, whereas the multiple interactions among the hybrid components create a flexible hydrogen-bonded supramolecular network and allow for solvent-unbreaking absorption to ensure the full participa- tion of the solvent and process stability. A mass solubility of NH3 up to 0.13 gg⁻¹ was achieved at 313 K and 101 kPa by the hybrid DES choline chloride/resorcinol/glycerol (1:3:5), which is higher than all reported ionic liquids and ordinary DESs. More- over, the performance remained the same after ten absorp- tion-desorption cycles and the DESs could be easily regenerat- ed. # Introduction Global challenges in environmental and sustainable chemistry have created a great demand for efficient uptake of NH3 from the gas phase, because NH3 is not only a major alkaline gaseous atmospheric pollutant and an important precursor of PM2.5 (particulate matter ≤2.5 µm), but also the dominant working medium in low-hazard Freon-free absorption refrigerators.[1] The omnipresent absorbents in current NH3 capture plants and refrigerators are water and aqueous inorganic or carboxylic acids, which have suffered from lots of longstanding problems.[2] First, the high volatility of water and many acids and the strong reactivity of NH3 with those solvents incurs significant difficulties to the desorption of NH3 and recycle of absorbents, making the energy-intensive distillation and a complex process usually indispensable in the plants and refrigerators.[3] Moreover, strong corrosion of equipment by the absorbents often occurs, and the wastewater discharge is hard to avoid. A lot of efforts have been exerted to address these problems, especially the utilization of ionic liquids as low-volatile solvents in absorption.[4] However, limited success has been achieved owing to the unsatisfactory mass solubility of NH3 [a] Y. [5] Thus far, it remains a big challenge to develop new materials for NH3 absorption to achieve both high NH3 solubility and superior recyclability along with environmental and synthetic merits. In recent years, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been put forward as a new class of solvents[6] that share the advantages of ultralow volatility and designability of ionic liquids and are superior in price, synthesis, and biodegradability.[6e] However, one chemical characteristic of DESs that is distinct from common solvents and ionic liquids is that they are supramolecular complexes of different individual components rather than a "pure" substance.[7] Therefore, DESs are more "fragile" liquids and their structure may decompose into individual components if there is a strong interaction with other solvents or solutes. Unfortunately, this fragile nature of DESs has not been paid enough attention up to now, although it is essential for their practical performance. An attempt to increase the efficiency of a DES for dissolving a solute by enhancing the DES-solute interactions, which is the common-sense strategy for ordinary solvents and ionic liquids, will probably fail because the enhanced DES-solute interactions may also break up the supramolecular structure of the DES and generate nonfunctional solids. This trade-off between the DES-solute interactions and the DES stability is particularly significant if the solute molecules are very active, as is the case for NH3 (Figure 1). Consequently, the trade-off between the DES–solute interactions and the DES stability is removed. An exceptional NH3 mass solubility of 0.13 gg⁻¹ at 313 K and 101 kPa was observed by the hybrid DES composed of choline chloride/resorcinol/glycerol (1:3:5; ChCl/Res/Gly), which was considerably higher than that of all reported ionic liquids and ordinary DESs. ## Results and Discussion ### NH3 absorption Several widely used ordinary DESs, which were binary mixtures of choline chloride (ChCl) and different hydrogen bond donors (HBDs), were first tested for the absorption of NH3 at 313 K and 101 kPa (Figure 1). White solids quickly appeared during the absorption by DESs with acidic HBDs (phenols and carboxylic acids), which severely inhibited the contact of NH3 with the remaining absorbent and prevented the continuation of the absorption process. FTIR measurement of these solids revealed that they were almost pure phenols (Figure 1 d, exemplified by the absorption of 1:3 ChCl/resorcinol), indicating that the solid formation is caused by the breaking up of the supramolecular structure in the DES. The adverse effect of this phenomenon is well demonstrated by the abnormal acidity-capacity relationship in the absorption by those solvents. Given that phenols and carboxylic acids are much more acidic than alcohols and urea, the NH3 uptake capacities of DESs containing phenols and carboxylic acids were expected to be higher than those of ChCl/Gly, ChCl/EG, and ChCl/Ur. However, these expected results were not observed. The NH3 uptake capacity of ChCl/PhA was lower than that of ChCl/Gly. Moreover, although resorcinol contains more hydroxy groups than phenol and is also more acidic (the respective pKa values of resorcinol and phenol are 9.44 and 9.94), the NH3 uptake capacity of ChCl/Res (0.053 g g¯¹) was unexpectedly much lower than that of ChCl/Phe (0.081 g g¯¹) owing to the more extensive formation of solids. This abnormal acidity-capacity relationship indicated that, because of the fragile supramolecular structure of DESs, the well-acknowledged strategy to enhance the solubility of basic solutes by increasing the acidity or the number of acidic groups of the solvents is not necessarily valid in the case of DESs. The use of neutral HBDs instead of phenols and carboxylic acids can prevent this structural breakage to ensure a “complete” absorption, but the reduced solute-solvent interactions also reduces the NH3 uptake capacity. To address the trade-off between the NH3-DES interaction and the supramolecular stability, we prepared a novel class of hybrid DESs, which was formed from a ternary mixture of chol- ine chloride, phenolic compounds, and polyalcohol and can be deemed as a hybrid of two binary DESs (choline chloride + phenolic compound and choline chloride + polyalcohol). Com- pared with ordinary DESs, the hybrid DESs reached a high level of NH3 solubility without the precipitation of solids. These results not only show the great potential of the synthesized DESs for the separation of NH₃ and CO₂, but are also for other processes in which a low CO₂ uptake capacity is preferred. ## Conclusions In this work, a new method to capture NH3 from gas phase with high efficiency has been proposed by using hybrid DESs as absorbents. The essence of this method is the construction of hybrid DESs with a flexible hydrogen-bonded supramolecular network, which enables the strong physical reversible solvation of NH3 and removes the need for a trade-off between the strength of the NH3–DES interactions and the stability of the supramolecular structure. Consequently, both exceptional NH3 mass capacity and excellent desorption–regeneration performance were achieved by this method, along with superb NH3/CO2 selectivity and environmental merit. Furthermore, taking into account their easy synthesis, relativity low cost, and good biocompatibility, the hybrid DESs have great potential as efficient and green alternatives to aqueous solvents and ionic liquids in practical NH3 capture and separation processes. These results not only show the great potential of the synthesized DESs for the separation of NH₃ and CO₂, but are also for other processes in which a low CO₂ uptake capacity is preferred. ## Conclusions In this work, a new method to capture NH3 from gas phase with high efficiency has been proposed by using hybrid DESs as absorbents. The essence of this method is the construction of hybrid DESs with a flexible hydrogen-bonded supramolecular network, which enables the strong physical reversible solvation of NH3 and removes the need for a trade-off between the strength of the NH3–DES interactions and the stability of the supramolecular structure. Consequently, both exceptional NH3 mass capacity and excellent desorption–regeneration performance were achieved by this method, along with superb NH3/CO2 selectivity and environmental merit. Furthermore, taking into account their easy synthesis, relativity low cost, and good biocompatibility, the hybrid DESs have great potential as efficient and green alternatives to aqueous solvents and ionic liquids in practical NH3 capture and separation processes. Additionally, considering that the fragility of the supramolecular structure is an intrinsic character of ordinary DESs, this work is also important for the application of DESs in more processes. # Experimental Section ## Chemicals and materials NH₃ (gas, 99.999%) and CO₂ (gas, 99.00%) were purchased from Jingong Special Gas Co., Ltd. Partial atomic charges were derived from the optimized geometry using the restrained electrostatic potential (RESP) method with the R.E.D.-III.4 package.[15] To control the pressure and temperature in the NPT ensemble, a name for the isothermal–iso- baric ensemble where the number of particles (N), pressure (P), and temperature (T) of the system are specified, the Berendsen barostat method with a relaxation time of 0.5 ps and the V-rescale thermostat method (313 K for all simulations) with a relaxation time of 0.1 ps were applied. The ChCl/Res/Gly simulation system was composed of 100 pairs of ChCl/Res/Gly (1:3:5 molar ratio). The ChCl/Res/Gly–NH3 simulation system was composed of 100 pairs of ChCl/Res/Gly–NH3 (1:3:5:7 molar ratio). An AMBER force field was adopted in this paper. The system was equilibrated for 2 ns in the NPT ensemble, and the last 1 ns was used to collect data for the radial distribution function and energy analysis. The forcefield pa- rameterization used in this work was validated through the com- parison of the predicted physical property, density, with the experi- mental value. The density of ChCl/Res/Gly obtained experimentally was approximately 1.21 gcm⁻³ at 313 K 101 kPa, whereas the den- sity obtained from MD was 1.24 g cm⁻³. Likewise, the experimental density of ChCl/Res/Gly–NH3 was approximately 1.14 g cm⁻³ at 313 K 101 kPa, whereas the density obtained from MD was 1.20 g cm⁻³. The deviation between the data was less than 7%, which is acceptable and shows the suitable performance of the used parameterization for describing the microscopic information. A complete listing of all the relevant force field parameters and partial charges is provided in Table S1.
